sections.description: This section summarizes the patient’s demographic background, acute complaints, relevant past medical history, physical examination findings, baseline laboratory abnormalities, and initial evaluation of hyponatraemia, setting the stage for the diagnostic process.
subtopics: Patient demographics, comorbidities (type 2 diabetes, undiagnosed) and occupational history
Acute symptoms: fever, headache, general malaise, loss of appetite, persistent hiccups, arthralgia
Mucocutaneous findings: oral aphthae, folliculitis‑like facial and truncal rash, evolving genital ulcer
Vital signs and volume status: febrile state, tachycardia, euvolemic appearance

Initial laboratory results: severe hyponatraemia, low serum osmolality, high urinary osmolality and Na, elevated ADH, markedly raised CRP and ESR, elevated CK, abnormal liver enzymes, hyperglycaemia, poor glycaemic control
Baseline imaging: normal CT head, chest and abdominal radiographs
Initial working diagnosis: suspected infection or systemic inflammatory disorder

sections.description: Here, we detail the broad spectrum of conditions considered for fever, headache and hyponatraemia, and the systematic investigations performed to rule them out, including infectious, neoplastic, autoimmune, endocrinological and other causes.
subtopics: Central nervous system infection: bacterial meningitis, viral encephalitis (HSV/VZV), tuberculous meningitis and their CSF laboratory profiles
CSF analysis results: mildly elevated opening pressure, protein, lymphocytic pleocytosis, negative cultures and PCR for common pathogens, absence of malignant cytology
Neoplastic work‑up: brain MRI findings, evaluation of sIL‑2R elevation, exclusion of CNS lymphoma or metastatic disease
Autoimmune/connective tissue disease screening: negative ANA, ENA panel, negative autoimmune serology, assessment of sarcoidosis with normal ACE and lysozyme levels
Endocrine causes of SIADH: assessment of hypothalamic involvement, medication review, pulmonary disease status, and exclusion of ectopic ADH sources
Laboratory testing strategy: CBC, cultures, viral PCR panels, fungal antigen, interferon‑γ release assay, endocrine evaluations
Interpretation of negative findings and their impact on narrowing the differential

sections.section_title: Diagnostic Reasoning & Confirmation of Behçet’s Disease with Neuro‑Behçet and SIADH
sections.description: This section integrates the cumulative data to arrive at a definitive diagnosis, outlining how the International Criteria for Behçet’s Disease were met, how aseptic meningitis was identified, and how SIADH was confirmed and linked to neuro‑Behçet’s.
subtopics: Application of the International Criteria for Behçet’s Disease: scoring of oral aphthae, genital ulcers, folliculitis‑like rash and absence of uveitis
Calculation of the total BC score (≥4) and designation of definite Behçet’s disease
Recognition of acute neuro‑Behçet’s disease: aseptic meningitis evidenced by CSF findings and normal MRI despite typical brainstem predilection
Diagnosis of SIADH: hyponatraemia with hypo‑osmolality, euvolemia, inappropriately concentrated urine, elevated urinary sodium, and supraphysiologic ADH level
Role of HLA‑B51 positivity in supporting the BD diagnosis but not required by criteria
Exclusion of alternative CNS inflammatory disorders after comprehensive evaluation
Correlation between CNS inflammation and SIADH pathogenesis (IL‑6 mediated ADH release hypothesis)

sections.section_title: Therapeutic Strategy and Management of Acute Neuro‑Behçet and SIADH
sections.description: This section outlines the treatment pathway, including initial empirical antimicrobial cover, the decision to forego corticosteroids, the use of colchicine as a monotherapy, and the focused management of SIADH with fluid restriction and monitoring.
subtopics: Empirical antimicrobial therapy (cefepime) started on admission and discontinued when cultures remained negative
Empirical antiviral therapy (acyclovir) started during CNS symptom flare and stopped after negative viral PCRs
Rationale for initiating colchicine monotherapy: neutrophil inhibition, IL‑1β/IL‑6 suppression, suitability for mucocutaneous and CNS inflammation
Avoidance of systemic corticosteroids given spontaneous recovery potential and patient preferences
SIADH management: strict fluid restriction (<800 mL/day), daily serum sodium monitoring, avoidance of rapid correction
Reasons for not using hypertonic saline or vasopressin receptor antagonists
Adjunct local therapies: topical corticosteroid ointment for aphthous lesions, silver sulfadiazine for genital ulcer
Rehabilitation measures for physical weakness secondary to systemic illness

sections.section_title: Outcome, Follow‑up, Clinical Lessons, and Implications for Practice
sections.description: This final section reviews the clinical course, long‑term management, and key take‑home messages for clinicians, emphasizing the potential role of colchicine in acute neuro‑Behçet’s and the importance of recognizing SIADH as an endocrine manifestation of CNS inflammation.
subtopics: Clinical timeline: fever resolution, appetite restoration, gradual improvement of headache, vertigo and hiccups, normalization of sodium and ADH within 16 days
Discharge after one‑month hospitalization and 4‑year colchicine therapy with no recurrence of mucocutaneous or neurological symptoms
Improvement of glycaemic control following stabilization of Behçet’s disease
Evidence that colchicine monotherapy may suffice for mild to moderate acute neuro‑Behçet’s and associated SIADH
Clinical implications: maintain high index of suspicion for neuro‑Behçet’s in febrile hyponatraemic patients with mucocutaneous lesions
Avoiding unnecessary cascade testing by focusing on clinically relevant markers (e.g., sIL‑2R, ACE) and interpreting them cautiously
Recognition that SIADH in CNS inflammation can manifest with nonspecific symptoms such as hiccups or rhabdomyolysis
Importance of interdisciplinary coordination (rheumatology, neurology, endocrinology) for holistic patient care
